strengths: Compelling motivation and design: Shifting from coarse, sample-level gradient/loss tracking to token-level representation matching effectively addresses sample-level length bias and loss-centric bias.

Substantial computational efficiency: Being forward-only and scoring at a single checkpoint makes TRIM considerably faster than gradient-based methods like LESS (4.40 hours vs. 35.76 hours on a 270k candidate pool) and trajectory-based methods like S2L.

Strong empirical performance: Matches or outperforms state-of-the-art baselines (LESS, TAGCOS) across standard benchmarks (MMLU, BBH, TyDiQA). The performance gain is particularly notable in low-topical-overlap downstream selection (GSM8K from a general pool, reaching 29.52% vs. LESS's 20.72%).

Thorough empirical evaluation: The paper includes extensive transfer experiments (across scale and architecture), length distribution analysis, target set noise/size robustness, in-domain selection on MathInstruct, and detailed ablations on architectural choices.
weaknesses: Heuristic nature of attention saliency: The convex combination of attention entropy (row) and received attention (column) is intuitively motivated and empirically validated, but lacks deeper theoretical analysis explaining why this specific proxy correlates with influence functions.

Heavy reliance on Nearest-Fingerprinted Fallback (NFF): Because the target set is small (5–10 examples), only a small fraction of the model vocabulary is observed in target fingerprints. Table 12 shows a significant drop in performance without NFF (from 49.43% down to 44.79%), indicating that embedding-space nearest-neighbor fallback does substantial heavy lifting.

Manual task-specific tuning for scoring scope: As discussed in Appendix C, selective token scoring (prompt-only vs. response-only vs. all) requires domain knowledge about whether the complexity lies in the prompt or response.

strengths: Compelling conceptual motivation: Shifting from coarse, sample-level gradient/loss tracking to token-level representation matching effectively addresses both computational efficiency (forward-only pass) and the pervasive issue of length bias in coreset selection.

Strong and rigorous empirical evaluation: The paper evaluates across diverse benchmarks (MMLU, BBH, TyDiQA, GSM8K, MATH, etc.), tests multiple model scales and families (LLaMA-2 7B/13B, LLaMA-3.1/3.2, Mistral-7B), reports mean and standard deviations across multiple runs, and compares against a wide set of strong baselines (e.g., LESS, TAGCOS, S2L).

Substantial computational speedup: By eliminating per-sample backward passes and checkpoint aggregation, TRIM reduces end-to-end selection wall-clock time from ~36 hours (LESS) to ~4.4 hours on a 270k candidate pool, as demonstrated by the theoretical and empirical cost analysis in Section 5.

Comprehensive analysis and ablations: The manuscript thoroughly examines failure modes and hyperparameters, including out-of-task robustness, target set size and noise sensitivity, pooling choices, layer aggregation depth, and dataset mixture distributions (Figure 4).
weaknesses: Slight notation inconsistency in score pooling: Equation (13) in the main text defines the robust sample score strictly as a combination of mean and maximum token scores ($w_\mu \mu + w_m m$), whereas Appendix C (Eq. 15) and Appendix H state that the default configuration includes an additional coverage bonus term ($η \kappa(c)$). Clarifying this discrepancy in the main methodology would improve readability.

Heavy reliance on Nearest-Fingerprinted Fallback (NFF): When using only 5–10 validation examples ($|T_{\text{val}}| \le 10$), only a minuscule fraction of the model's vocabulary is directly fingerprinted; the vast majority of tokens in candidate samples must rely on NFF backoff via input embedding cosine similarity. While Table 12 and Table 15 show reasonable robustness, a deeper quantitative discussion of what percentage of candidate tokens trigger NFF and how this affects representational quality across different vocabularies would strengthen the paper.

Attribution of the large gain on GSM8K: On GSM8K (Table 2), TRIM outperforms LESS by ~8.8% (29.52% vs 20.72%). Figure 4 reveals that TRIM selects predominantly from the CoT subset (~80%) for GSM8K, whereas LESS selects heavily from Flan-v2. It would be valuable to discuss more explicitly whether this dramatic gain is driven primarily by matching specific Chain-of-Thought delimiter tokens/connectives or deeper semantic reasoning patterns.

strengths: High Computational Efficiency: TRIM operates entirely via forward passes using a single warmed-up checkpoint, eliminating the prohibitive per-sample backward passes required by gradient-based influence methods (e.g., LESS, TAGCOS). This results in substantial wall-clock speedups (e.g., 4.4 hours vs. 35.8 hours for LESS on a 270k pool).

Principled Mitigation of Length Bias: By scoring at the token level via attention-derived saliency and robust pooling (mean + max + coverage), the method avoids the systematic bias toward short sequences that frequently degrades sample-level gradient and loss-based selection methods.

Strong and Consistent Empirical Results: Across general reasoning benchmarks (MMLU, BBH, TyDiQA), challenging low-overlap transfer (GSM8K from non-math data), and in-domain math curation (MATHINSTRUCT), TRIM consistently matches or outperforms prior state-of-the-art coreset methods.

Extensive Evaluation and Ablations: The paper provides comprehensive empirical validation, including cross-architecture/cross-scale transferability (LLaMA-2-7B to 13B and Mistral-7B; LLaMA-3.2-1B to LLaMA-3.1-8B), robustness to target set size and noise, and detailed ablations on architectural choices (layer depth, pooling functions, fallback penalties).
weaknesses: Modest Gains on General Benchmarks: While TRIM demonstrates large gains in specific settings like low-overlap transfer to GSM8K, the performance improvements over the strongest baseline (LESS) on general multi-task benchmarks are relatively incremental (e.g., 48.56% vs. 48.27% average across MMLU, BBH, and TyDiQA in Table 1; and slightly below S2L on MATHINSTRUCT in Table 20).

Space Mismatch in Nearest-Fingerprint Fallback: For tokens unobserved in the target set, the fallback mechanism (Eq. 11) identifies the nearest token class in the static input-embedding space, but subsequently computes cosine similarity against fingerprints derived from last-layer hidden states (Eq. 12). Because representations evolve significantly across layers, geometry in input-embedding space may not faithfully preserve similarity in deep hidden-state space.

Representation Averaging Across Contexts: Collapsing all contextual occurrences of a token class into a single prototype fingerprint vector (Eq. 9) risks conflating distinct semantic senses and syntactic roles of polysemous words.

Heuristic Hyperparameter Tuning: The overall scoring function relies on several heuristic weights and hyperparameters (e.g., attention weights $w_Q, w_K$, pooling weights $w_\mu, w_m$, fallback penalty $\lambda$, and coverage weight $\eta$), although the sensitivity analyses in Appendix H partially alleviate this concern.

strengths: Sound motivation: Moving from sample-level, loss/gradient-based data selection to token-level representation matching effectively addresses both computational efficiency (by avoiding backward passes and multi-checkpoint caching) and the length bias inherent in sequence-level aggregation.

Strong and consistent empirical performance: TRIM consistently outperforms competitive baselines (e.g., LESS, TAGCOS, S2L) across multiple benchmarks (CommonsenseQA, SocialiQA, HellaSwag). Notably, in the out-of-domain GSM8K setting (Table 2), TRIM reaches 29.52% exact match with a 5% coreset—substantially outperforming the next-best method LESS (20.72%) and approaching full-data fine-tuning (30.25%).

Cross-model and cross-architecture transferability: Demonstrating that a 5% coreset curated with a small 1B proxy model matches or outperforms the in-model oracle when fine-tuning larger 7B/8B models (Llama-3.1-8B and Mistral-7B) makes the framework practically useful for budget-constrained training pipelines.

Thorough analytical insights and ablations: The paper provides informative analyses regarding coreset length distribution (Figure 3), task-adaptive dataset composition (Figures 4 and 5), and systematic ablations on key components (OOV penalty, pooling functions, layers used, checkpoint timing in Table 8).
weaknesses: Reliance on vocabulary-level fingerprinting with very few target samples: A target validation set of only 5–10 examples covers only a tiny fraction of the model's vocabulary (a few hundred tokens out of 32k–128k). As a result, the candidate scoring stage heavily relies on nearest-neighbor backoff in embedding space (Eq. 11–12) for the majority of token types. While this works empirically, deeper analysis into the stability and variance across different random draws of target validation sets would strengthen the paper.

Discrepancy in scoring formulation between main text and appendix: Equation 13 in the main text defines candidate scoring purely as a linear combination of mean and max token similarities, whereas Appendix B.1 (Eq. 15) reveals that the actual implementation relies on an additional coverage regularizer $\eta \kappa(c)$ (with $\eta = 0.05$ noted in Table 8). This component should be properly stated and integrated into Section 3.2.

Lack of reported wall-clock / GPU-hour measurements: While the theoretical complexity analysis in Section 5 clearly demonstrates asymptotic advantages ($O(fN)$ vs $O(3fNC)$), empirical wall-clock times or throughput comparisons against LESS and TAGCOS under identical hardware would provide concrete evidence for the 'orders of magnitude faster' claim in practice.

strengths: Compelling motivation: Shifting from computationally expensive, gradient-based data influence estimation (e.g., LESS, TAGCOS) to an efficient, forward-only selection method addresses a critical practical bottleneck in instruction tuning coreset curation.

Promising empirical gains: Across general-domain multiple-choice reasoning benchmarks (CommonsenseQA, SocialiQA, HellaSwag) and an out-of-domain mathematical reasoning setting (GSM8K), TRIM demonstrates consistent improvements over competitive baselines, even outperforming full-data fine-tuning in certain settings.

Cross-model and cross-architecture transferability: Results in Table 3 show that coresets curated with a lightweight 1B parameter scorer transfer effectively to larger targets (Llama-3.1-8B and Mistral-7B), which is practically valuable for resource-constrained fine-tuning pipelines.

Mitigation of length bias: The empirical analysis in Section 4.4 and Figure 3 shows that TRIM selects longer, structurally rich sequences compared to gradient-norm-based methods that tend to suffer from length confounding.
weaknesses: Missing ablation on the central mechanism (attention-derived saliency): The paper claims that attention-derived token saliency (integrating row entropy and column hubness) is key to its success. However, Table 8 ablates checkpoint choices, layer count, and pooling strategies, but fails to ablate the saliency weights themselves (i.e., comparing $\alpha_i$ against uniform weighting $\alpha_i = 1$, row-only, or column-only saliency). Without this baseline, it remains unclear whether the attention saliency heuristic provides meaningful signal over simple unweighted token hidden state matching.

Heuristic OOV handling given extremely small validation sets: The target validation set $T_{val}$ consists of only 5–10 examples, covering only a tiny fraction of the model's vocabulary. Consequently, the vast majority of tokens in candidate samples must fall back to the nearest fingerprinted class via input embedding cosine similarity (Eq. 11–12). The semantic validity of comparing last-layer contextual hidden states $h_{c,j}$ to a fingerprint $f_{\bar{t}_j}$ mapped via static input embeddings is questionable and theoretically underspecified.

Lack of wall-clock runtime and empirical throughput benchmarks: While Section 5 outlines asymptotic FLOP complexities, the paper omits empirical wall-clock runtimes and memory consumption on the 270k candidate dataset (Section F.3 explicitly states they do not report wall-clock time). Given that efficiency is a primary motivation, empirical benchmarking against LESS and forward-only baselines is necessary.

Limited evaluation diversity: The downstream evaluation is restricted to multiple-choice benchmarks and GSM8K. There are no evaluations on open-ended generation, code generation (e.g., HumanEval/MBPP), or chat benchmarks (e.g., MT-Bench/AlpacaEval), leaving the generalizability of the method to general instruction-following tasks unverified.

strengths: Novel token-centric perspective: Instead of relying on computationally heavy sample-level gradients or loss trajectories, TRIM introduces a forward-only framework that builds token-level fingerprints via attention-derived saliency (combining row-wise attention sharpness and column-wise received attention).

High computational efficiency at scoring time: Because Stage II only requires forward evaluation without per-sample backward passes or multi-checkpoint tracking, candidate scoring scales linearly as O(fN), offering substantial scalability advantages over gradient-based influence methods like LESS.

Comprehensive empirical analyses: The paper provides insightful qualitative and diagnostic evaluations, including demonstration of length bias mitigation (Figure 3), task-adaptive data selection behavior (Figure 4 / Figure 5), and cross-model / cross-scale transferability from a 1B scorer to 7B/8B models (Table 3).

Impressive performance on low-overlap reasoning transfer: On GSM8K selection from a general-purpose instruction pool, TRIM achieves 29.52% accuracy (nearly matching full-data fine-tuning at 30.25% and outperforming LESS by ~8.8%).
weaknesses: Absence of empirical wall-clock and memory measurements: Although computational efficiency is a core motivation and contribution, the authors explicitly state in Appendix F.3 that they do not report wall-clock time or GPU-hours, providing only asymptotic big-O complexity in Table 4. Concrete empirical runtime comparisons against LESS, TAGCOS, and forward-only baselines across scoring and selection phases are essential to validate practical speedups.

Heuristic fragility of token fingerprinting with small validation sets: In Stage I, T_val contains only 5–10 examples, covering only a tiny fraction of the vocabulary (at most a few hundred token types). For all other tokens, the method relies on nearest-neighbor fallback in the static input-embedding space. Notably, Table 8 indicates that the default penalty parameter is lambda = 1.0 (no penalty), meaning arbitrary out-of-vocabulary tokens are mapped to target fingerprints without downweighting. Furthermore, the paper does not evaluate variance across different random draws of T_val to show robustness to sample selection noise.

Selective baselines and architectural inconsistency in out-of-domain evaluation: While Table 1 tests eight baselines on LLaMA-3.2-1B, Table 2 suddenly switches backbones to LLaMA-2-7B without clear motivation and omits lexical/n-gram retrieval baselines (BM25, DSIR) and representation-based baselines (RDS). Given that GSM8K heavily benefits from retrieving Chain-of-Thought (CoT) data, comparing against BM25/DSIR is crucial to verify whether simple keyword/n-gram matching achieves similar subset shifts.

Modest performance improvements on standard multiple-choice benchmarks: In Table 1, the margin over LESS on HellaSwag is negligible (+0.07%, well within the standard deviation of 0.1%), and overall gains across CommonsenseQA and SocialiQA average ~1.15%, indicating that the large claimed gains ('up to 9%') are driven almost entirely by the single GSM8K setup.
